title: Data Science Examples
description: Small Data Science examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Begin with a clear question
examples.description: Data is recorded information. Data science uses careful questions and checks to learn from it. A clear question tells us what we need to count.
examples.code:
Question: which book type was borrowed most this week?
Needed: one row per borrowing and the book type
Not needed: learner names or home addresses
Result: a count for each type

examples.title: Organise rows and columns
examples.description: A row holds one record. A column holds one kind of information. A list of dictionaries can represent a small table in Python.

examples.title: Read a tiny CSV table
examples.description: CSV stores table rows as text, often with commas between fields. A CSV reader handles fields more carefully than splitting every line yourself.
examples.code:
import csv
from io import StringIO
text = "type,count\nstory,4\nscience,2\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(StringIO(text)))
print(rows[0]["count"])

examples.title: Use consistent units
examples.description: Before comparing measurements, put them in the same units. Metres and centimetres describe length on different scales.
examples.code:
lengths_cm = [100, 150, 200]
lengths_m = [value / 100 for value in lengths_cm]
print(lengths_m)

examples.title: Handle missing values honestly
examples.description: A missing value means a measurement is absent. It does not mean zero. Keep track of what you leave out of a calculation.
examples.code:
minutes = [10, None, 20]
known = [value for value in minutes if value is not None]
print(sum(known) / len(known), len(known))

examples.title: Check duplicate records
examples.description: A duplicate is a repeated record. Some repeats are mistakes, but repeated events can also be real. Use a suitable identifier before removing anything.
examples.code:
events = [{"id": "a", "type": "story"}, {"id": "a", "type": "story"}, {"id": "b", "type": "story"}]
ids = [row["id"] for row in events]
print(len(ids), len(set(ids)))

examples.title: Count categories
examples.description: A category is a named group. Counter counts how often each value occurs in a list.
examples.code:
from collections import Counter
borrowings = ["story", "science", "story", "poetry"]
counts = Counter(borrowings)
print(counts["story"], counts["science"])

examples.title: Mean and median show different centres
examples.description: The mean adds values and divides by their count. The median is the middle value after sorting. A very large value can pull the mean upward.
examples.code:
from statistics import mean, median
minutes = [2, 3, 4, 5, 36]
print(mean(minutes), median(minutes))

examples.title: Look at spread
examples.description: Spread describes how far apart values are. The range subtracts the smallest value from the largest. It is a simple start, not a full description.

examples.title: Choose a clear chart
examples.description: A chart should fit the question. Bars compare category counts. A line can show ordered measurements over time. Labels must name the values and units.
examples.code:
Question: compare borrowings by book type
Chart: bars
Horizontal labels: story, science, poetry
Vertical label: number of borrowings
Bar baseline: zero

examples.title: A pattern does not prove a cause
examples.description: Two things can change together without one causing the other. A third factor or the way data was collected may explain the pattern.
examples.code:
Observed: more ice cream sales and more swimming on hot days
Possible shared cause: warm weather
Unsupported claim: buying ice cream makes people swim

examples.title: Report the answer and its limits
examples.description: A useful report states the question, result, method and limits. Readers should be able to check where the answer came from.
examples.code:
Question: which type was borrowed most this week?
Sample: 4 fictional borrowing events
Result: story had 2 events; science and poetry had 1 each
Limit: one tiny week does not describe the whole year
